comparison: Both strongly support the biochemical characterization of sUA as a CD38 inhibitor (C40-C46). OpenEval emphasizes enzyme kinetics and Ki values with physiological relevance. Peer reviewers call the data 'very solid' and affirm the inhibition constants support physiological inhibition. OpenEval also covers reversibility (C47-C48) which peer review includes in the same evaluation.

OpenEval separately evaluates reversibility claims (C47-C48) as supported by dilution experiments. Peer review groups these with the main biochemical characterization (C40-C46) and accepts them without specific challenge as part of the 'very solid' biochemical data.

Both support the specificity testing of purine metabolites (C50-C55). OpenEval emphasizes comprehensive testing at supraphysiological concentrations. Peer review accepts this as part of 'convincing evidence' from 'different approaches' without raising concerns about the specificity characterization.

Both support the structure-activity relationship studies identifying the functional group (C56-C62). OpenEval details the systematic testing of analogs and the requirement for both structural elements. Peer review treats this structural analysis as part of the solid biochemical characterization supporting main findings.

Both support cellular NAD+ findings (C63-C68). OpenEval notes strong evidence for CD38 as primary target but suggests CD38 knockdown controls would strengthen conclusions. Peer reviewers accept the data as 'very solid' and of 'extreme importance' without requesting additional controls, treating the evidence as sufficient.

Both support in vivo NAD+ effects in the uricase inhibitor model (C78-C81). OpenEval emphasizes genotype-dependent effects as compelling genetic evidence. Peer review accepts this as part of data showing sUA affects 'NAD+ levels both in vitro and in vivo' with 'very solid' data, also covering reversibility and mechanism claims (C82, C89-C92).

OpenEval supports time-course reversibility data (C89-C91) while noting direct gene expression measurement would strengthen the transcriptional exclusion claim. Peer review groups this with other in vivo NAD+ data and accepts it without challenge as part of the 'very solid' evidence.

OpenEval supports in vitro reconstitution showing CD38 sufficiency (C92). Peer review includes this as part of the accepted in vivo mechanistic evidence, treating it as supporting detail for the CD38-mediated effects demonstrated across multiple approaches.

Both support NMN degradation inhibition findings (C103-C106). OpenEval emphasizes genetic and rescue experiments as strong evidence. Peer review notes the BMDM limitation for inflammasome validation but does not directly challenge the NMN degradation data itself, treating it as supporting mechanistic detail.

Both strongly support the inflammasome cytokine findings in the cLPS model (C122-C125). OpenEval emphasizes specificity for IL-1β/IL-18 vs TNF-α and genotype-dependence. Peer reviewers describe this as a key finding with 'significant implications for inflammation' and accept the CD38-dependence demonstrated by KO mice.

Both support the peritonitis model data (C130-C133). OpenEval notes consistency with cLPS model and strong genetic controls. Peer review accepts this as evidence from 'different approaches' supporting the main conclusions about sUA, CD38, NAD+, and inflammatory responses without raising specific concerns.

Both support the uricase inhibitor model characterization (C71-C77). OpenEval notes OA assessment is reasonable but direct CD38 activity measurement would strengthen conclusions. Peer review accepts the model while acknowledging limitations, noting authors appropriately discuss constraints and made revisions to improve the manuscript.

OpenEval rates claims about cADPR under inflammatory conditions (C82-C83) as uncertain, noting the compensation hypothesis is speculative. Peer review groups C82 with other in vivo NAD+ data (C78-C81, C89-C92) and accepts it as part of the 'very solid' evidence without specifically addressing the mechanistic speculation in C83.

OpenEval rates tissue-level NAD+ effects and saturation hypothesis (C93-C96) as uncertain, noting variable effects and need for validation of indirect mechanisms. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses these tissue-level claims.

OpenEval rates metabolic reprogramming and sirtuin hypotheses (C86-C88) as uncertain, noting speculation without direct demonstration. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses these compensatory mechanism claims.

OpenEval rates explanations for negative NMN results in certain conditions (C100-C102) as uncertain, noting reliance on citations rather than direct measurements. Peer review notes the inability to validate findings in BMDMs as a weakness but focuses on inflammasome validation rather than the NMN-specific mechanistic explanations.

OpenEval supports BMDM uptake findings (C110-C113) while noting direct intracellular sUA manipulation would strengthen conclusions. Peer review rates this as uncertain, identifying low sUA uptake in BMDMs as a 'significant weakness' that prevents validation of in vivo findings, emphasizing need for genetic evidence and direct inflammasome assessment.

OpenEval supports THP-1 cell data (C115-C117) as complementing BMDM data and suggesting cell-type differences. Peer review acknowledges 'pharmacological blockage in THP-1 cells provides mechanistic evidence' but emphasizes this is insufficient, stating 'genetic evidence and direct assessment of inflammasome components would be necessary to fully validate the model.'

OpenEval supports dose-dependent cLPS findings (C127-C129) showing limitations of CD38-sUA axis at high doses. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses these dose-response limitations.

OpenEval rates chemokine mechanism claims (C134-C135) as uncertain, noting multiple alternative explanations for reduced cell recruitment. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses these mechanistic interpretations.

OpenEval supports control experiments addressing confounding effects of compounds used to elevate sUA (C144-C147). No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses these control experiments.
OpenEval supports endogenous sUA measurement controls (C49). No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses this methodological control.

OpenEval supports specificity data showing minimal effects of other purines at physiological concentrations (C69-C70). No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses these specificity controls.
OpenEval supports controls distinguishing sUA from MSU crystal effects (C118-C121). No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses this important methodological distinction.
OpenEval supports background/rationale claims (C1-C15) as appropriately cited. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses these introductory claims.
OpenEval supports discovery approach description (C16-C20). No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses the initial screening methodology.
OpenEval supports CD38 background claims (C21-C31) as appropriately cited. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses this background information.

OpenEval rates claims about additional targets at high sUA concentrations (C139-C140) as uncertain due to speculation. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses these claims about concentration-dependent mechanisms.
OpenEval supports exclusion of inosine as major contributor (C141-C143). No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses this potential confounding factor.

Both strongly support the main conclusions (C149-C150). OpenEval states CD38 as direct target is well-supported by enzyme kinetics and functional roles demonstrated by multiple experiments. Peer reviewers call it 'an important advance' with 'significant implications' and 'major implications to understanding aging diseases,' describing findings as 'of extreme importance.'

Peer review addresses model limitations and author responses to revision (C71, C73-C74, C192-C193), noting authors 'discuss the main limitations' and 'made changes to improve the manuscript.' OpenEval R12 partially overlaps on C71, C73-C74 but does not address the revision process or claims C192-C193.
